title: Cortical Over-Recruitment in Cerebral Palsy as the Upward Projection of Lower-Layer Functional Vacancy: A Hypothesis from the Evolutionary Information Layering Framework
content: Studies using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) have repeatedly shown that children with cerebral palsy (CP) recruit more cortex during motor tasks than typically developing peers: activation is stronger, spreads beyond the primary sensorimotor region, loses its normal lateralization, and often reaches the prefrontal cortex. This finding has been replicated across fine hand movements, bimanual coordination, balance tasks, and gait, yet it remains without an agreed interpretation. Five accounts circulate in the literature (compensation, reduced cortical inhibition, dedifferentiation, inefficiency, and cognitive compensation), but each explains only part of the data, and none offers a way to decide when extra cortical activity is helping the child and when it is not. This paper reinterprets the phenomenon using the Evolutionary Information Layering (EIL) framework, in which the nervous system is organized as a stack of layers laid down across evolution and development, each preferentially handling the functions assigned to it. We argue that over-recruitment in CP is best understood as the upward projection of lower-layer functional vacancy: when subcortical modules that normally automate rhythm, synergy, and postural adjustment are disconnected from descending control, the details of movement are handed up to the cortex for explicit processing. On this view the five existing accounts can be read as descriptions of the same mechanism observed at different levels, which offers a possible route past their long-standing disagreement. The interpretation yields testable predictions, including a task-dependent gradient of over-recruitment, a reduction of cortical load under standardized passive movement, and a redistribution rather than a simple reduction of activation after effective training. It also suggests two quantitative indices, a hierarchical shift index and a synchronization-desynchronization separation index, that can be computed from ordinary fNIRS recordings. We discuss how these ideas translate into an experimental program and what they would mean for assessment and treatment selection in pediatric neurorehabilitation.
